content: Allergies and food reactions are common in infants and children and can be triggered by various foods, including cow's milk-based formulas. Soy-based formulas have been used as a treatment for infants with allergies or food intolerances. However, it remains uncertain whether soy formulas can prevent allergies or food intolerances in infants who do not already show clinical signs of these conditions. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether feeding infants an adapted soy formula, as compared to human milk, cow's milk formula, or hydrolyzed protein formula, could prevent the development of allergies or food intolerances in infants without pre-existing clinical evidence of these conditions. To address this question, a systematic search was conducted using the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group's standard search strategy. Databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL were searched up to March 2006. Previous reviews and cross-references were also examined. The inclusion criteria required randomized or quasi-randomized trials comparing soy formula to other feeding options in infants during their first six months of life. Only studies with at least 80% follow-up of participants and proper reporting of group assignments were included. The primary outcomes assessed were the development of clinical allergies, specific allergies, and food intolerances. Data were analyzed using either a fixed-effect model or a random-effects model, depending on the presence of heterogeneity in treatment effects. Three studies met the inclusion criteria, all of which enrolled high-risk infants with a family history of allergies in a first-degree relative. None of the studies included infants fed human milk, and none examined the effects of short-term soy formula feeding. Instead, all studies compared prolonged soy formula feeding to cow's milk formula feeding. One study was methodologically sound and did not include unbalanced allergy-preventing interventions between treatment groups. Another study, which had unclear allocation concealment and a 19.5% loss to follow-up, reported a significant reduction in infant allergy, asthma, and allergic rhinitis. However, no other study demonstrated significant benefits from soy formula use. Meta-analysis revealed no significant differences in the incidence of childhood allergies (two studies; relative risk [RR] 0.73, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.37–1.44). Similarly, no significant differences were found in infant asthma (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.86–1.40), infant eczema (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.95–1.52), childhood eczema prevalence (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.73–1.68), infant rhinitis (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.76–1.16), or childhood rhinitis prevalence (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.73–2.00). Further meta-analyses showed no significant differences in the incidence of childhood asthma (three studies, 728 infants; RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.26–1.92), childhood eczema (two studies, 283 infants; RR 1.57, 95% CI 0.90–2.75), or childhood rhinitis (two studies, 283 infants; RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.06–8.00). One study reported no significant differences in the incidence of cow's milk protein intolerance (CMPI) in infants (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.45–2.62), cow's milk allergy (CMA) in infants (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.24–4.86), childhood soy protein allergy (RR 3.26, 95% CI 0.36–29.17), or urticaria. No study compared soy formula to hydrolyzed protein formula. In conclusion, feeding infants with soy formula cannot be recommended as a strategy to prevent allergies or food intolerances in those at high risk for these conditions. Further research may be necessary to explore the potential role of soy formulas in preventing allergies or food intolerances in infants who cannot be breastfed and have a strong family history of allergies or cow's milk protein intolerance.
